subject: Australia
note: Cited to pinned Wikipedia revisions (trusted_secondary): Dingo Fence, Dalby, Queensland and Cameron Corner Survey Marker. The page gives the fence's two ends only by name (Jimbour near Dalby; cliffs above the Great Australian Bight near Nundroo) and no path, so the map draws no line for the fence: it marks Cameron Corner (the page's own coordinates) and a point at Dalby, which is the page's coordinate for the town near the start, not for Jimbour itself. Nundroo has no coordinates on its page, so it is not marked; the Great Australian Bight is labelled from the map data. The page's claim that the fence was set up so that landowners 'could legally keep First Nations people off the land' is a contested historical reading and is left out. Ecologists' views are attributed to the page.

claims.text: The Dingo Fence stretches 5,614 km from Jimbour on the Darling Downs near Dalby, through arid land, to cliffs of the Nullarbor Plain above the Great Australian Bight near Nundroo; it is the longest fence in the world.

The fence is a pest-exclusion fence to keep dingoes out of the relatively fertile south-east part of Australia, where they have largely been exterminated, and to protect the sheep flocks of southern Queensland.
The fence was built from 1880 to 1885 (infobox: built 1880–85).
The fence passes Cameron Corner, the point where the three states of Queensland, New South Wales and South Australia meet.
The 2,500 km section of the fence in Queensland is also known as the Great Barrier Fence or Wild Dog Barrier Fence.

Mike Letnic of the University of New South Wales found that where dingoes had been excluded by the fence, biodiversity was reduced, with fewer native mammals; ecologists quoted on the page call the fence a colonial legacy that is more harmful than helpful.
In December 2023 construction began on a 32 km extension to close the gap between the New South Wales and South Australian border fences; the extension was completed in 2025.
